chapters.summary: Speaker Julie Menin acknowledges Councilmember Brooks-Powers, then discusses the Saturday homeowner tour at York College with the deputy speaker. She highlights efforts to combat deed theft, predatory loans, home repairs, storm proofing, and foreclosure assistance under the $5.5 million Homeowner Stabilization Services Initiative.
chapters.title: Menin opens with homeowner tour and stabilization initiative

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Councilmember Silvina Brooks-Powers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, so there is always an issue that the council is working on to improve our city.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And on Saturday, the deputy speaker and I kicked off our homeowner tour at York College,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: helping to combat deed theft and predatory loans, as well as assistance with home repairs and storm proofing and foreclosure assistance.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's a part of our $5.5 million commitment to the new Homeowner Stabilization Services Initiative, which will help residents preserve their properties.

chapters.summary: Menin says free 2K will be available to every school district in the Bronx and Staten Island by fall 2027. She notes this will give 10,000 more children access and save thousands of parents child care costs.
chapters.title: Menin announces free 2K expansion for Bronx and Staten Island

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: On Monday, together with the mayor and the governor, we were so proud to be there to announce that free 2K

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: will be available to every school district in the Bronx and Staten Island by the fall of 2027.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And that expands.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: means, of course, an additional 10,000 children will have a shot at a brighter future and thousands more parents won't have to empty their pockets to pay for child care.

chapters.summary: Menin recounts Tuesday's hearing on EMS response times. She says the department is underfunded, staffing is inadequate, and New Yorkers wait over 13 minutes on average for life-threatening emergencies, which is too high for cardiac arrest cases.
chapters.title: Menin highlights EMS response time hearing and staffing crisis

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: On Tuesday, we held a hearing on the response times of our EMS services.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The department is currently underfunded, leading to significantly inadequate staffing that poses deadly consequences.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Currently, a New Yorker must wait an average of more than 13 minutes for life-threatening emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And for those that are in cardiac arrest, when literally every second counts, let alone every minute, that number is simply far too high.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We must, we absolutely must pay those who provide a life-saving service a living wage and ensure that New Yorkers in crisis can access the care that they need.

chapters.summary: Menin announces a street co-naming, Champions Plaza, honoring the seven championships won by the Knicks and Rangers. She jokes about the Knicks' opening night loss and says today is a different day.
chapters.title: Menin unveils Champions Plaza street co-naming for Knicks and Rangers

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Ahead of the switching gears, ahead of the opening night for the Knicks, we unveiled a street co-naming, Champions Plaza, in honor of the seven championships that were won by our home teams, the Knicks and the Rangers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And while it didn't go New York's way on Tuesday, today is a different day.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The City Council has plenty of victories to celebrate on behalf of New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Menin says the Council will vote to raise the income eligibility limit for the Senior Citizen Rent Increase Exemption and Disability Rent Increase Exemption programs to $75,000. She notes this is a meaningful increase from the $50,000 cap set in 2015 and will help seniors and disabled New Yorkers stay in their homes.
chapters.title: Menin announces vote to raise SCRIE/DRIE income limit to $75,000

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So today we are going to vote on raising the income eligibility limit to 75.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: $5,000 for the Senior Citizen Rent Increase Exemption Program, SCRI, and the Disability Rent Increase Exemption Program, DRE.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This is a truly meaningful difference from the current cap of $50,000, which it has been since 2015.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This program, which freezes rent for eligible senior citizens and disabled New Yorkers while still giving landlords a tax credit,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: will provide major relief to those residents, assuring them that they can stay in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's just one of many of the initiatives that the Council has proposed to make New York more affordable and livable for everyone.

chapters.summary: Menin says the Council aims to pass Romantia's law, making history after 19 years of attempts. She notes the first bill was introduced by then-Councilmember Tony Avella and that past councils and mayors tried but failed to pass it.
chapters.title: Menin frames horse carriage ban as 19-year animal welfare and public safety fight

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we certainly hope to have another victory to celebrate a fight we have been engaged in since 2007.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And that fight is for animal welfare and for public safety.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: For people's lives and people's livelihoods.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So today we aim to pass Romantia's law.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And by doing so, I want to be clear, we are going to make history.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: For 19 years, mayors and speakers alike have tried to convert this idea into reality.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I know that this has been a long time coming, over 19 years ago that the first bill was introduced by Councilmember then Tony Avella into the Council.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But certainly past councils tried to do this, but was not able to.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But this Council is delivering.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Council is listening to the voices of New Yorkers, and this council is squaring our actions with our speeches.

chapters.summary: Menin says Ramach Mahajan's death was one death too many and a turning point. She argues the law passed in his name will prevent the next tragedy and proves the Council's commitment to public safety.
chapters.title: Menin cites Ramach Mahajan's death as turning point for horse carriage law

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: When Ramach Mahajan was taken from his family, from our city, from the world, it was a turning point.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And Ramach's death was one death too many.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And the law that we are going to pass in his name will prevent the next one.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So today proves that our commitment to making New York safer and more livable is deeper than the words we are willing to say in the wake of a tragedy.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And it symbolizes the substance of our actions when we live up to that commitment.

chapters.summary: Menin outlines the bill's June 2028 phase-out deadline, industry transition framework, and humane treatment requirements. She says horse owners can keep their horses but cannot transfer them for slaughter, and the administration will help over 150 drivers find new jobs through training, counseling, and referrals.
chapters.title: Menin details horse carriage phase-out, worker transition, and humane treatment

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Ramont's law sets a June 2028 phase-out deadline, and it creates a detailed industry transition framework.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It is going to ensure that the horses themselves receive humane treatment wherever they go next, requiring certification that horses will not be transferred for slaughter

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: or even allowing horse owners to, and it even allows horse owners to keep their horses if they so choose.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's going to support the transition for the more than 150 active horse carriage drivers because we want to make sure that they are protected.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We will help find them new jobs over the next two years.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That is something that the administration will do under the bill, including providing civil service trainings, career counseling, assistance.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: accessing education and referrals to other employment opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The bill also requires administration to consider establishing a compensation program.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And the council is very committed to working with the administration throughout this very important transition period.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So certainly from a small movement that started nearly two centuries ago to an initial city council attempt that energized the effort nearly two decades ago

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: to today, where we are bringing that effort finally to fruition for the horses, for our safety, and for our city.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And that is a promise that we are now making a reality.

chapters.summary: Menin lists land use items: 48-50 Convent Avenue Cluster ANCP for 77 affordable homeownership units, 1455 Coney Island Avenue rezoning for a nine-story long-term care facility, and 135-27 Sapphire Street rezoning for a six-story building.
chapters.title: Menin outlines land use items for vote

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So now let's proceed with more details about this afternoon's stated meeting.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: First, we'll vote on the following land use items.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: 48-50 Convent Avenue Cluster ANCP will support the conversion of four city-owned rental buildings to 77 affordable home ownership units

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: and two superintendent units in Majority Leader Sean Abreu's district.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: 1455 Coney Island Avenue rezoning will facilitate the development of a nine-story long-term care facility with 300 patient beds in Councilmember Simka Felder's district.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: 135-27 Sapphire Street rezoning will facilitate the development of one six-story building in Council

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: member Joanne Areola's district.

chapters.summary: Menin lists finance items including Resolution 666-A on business improvement district expenditures, a transparency resolution on expense budget designations, and pre-considered resolutions granting 40-year tax exemptions for buildings in several districts.
chapters.title: Menin outlines finance items for vote

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Next, we're going to vote on the following finance items.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Resolution 666-A, which is sponsored by Councilmember Linda Lee, would set the date, time, and place for the hearing on the local law that would increase the annual expenditure for eight business improvement districts.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: A transparency resolution approving new designations and changes in the designation of certain organizations receiving funding in the expense budget.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And several pre-considered resolutions sponsored by Councilmember Linda Lee that would grant a partial 40-year tax exemption under Article 11 of the Private Housing Finance Law

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: for buildings in the District of Councilmembers Carr-Wilson, Elsie Encarnacion, Oswald Filaes, and Justin Sanchez, and Deputy Speaker Dr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Natasha Williams.

chapters.summary: Menin lists legislation: Resolution 650 opposing federal Head Start rule changes, Resolution 625B declaring October Reggaeton Heritage Month, Intro 927-A renaming Shorefront Parkway to Edgemere Avenue, and Intro 786A on ballot curing for voters in DOC custody.
chapters.title: Menin lists legislation on today's agenda

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Today, we will also vote on the following pieces of legislation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Resolution 650, sponsored by Councilmember Jennifer Gutierrez, would oppose the federally proposed rule change titled

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs and call on the federal government to prioritize protecting and growing access to high-quality education for young children.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Resolution 625B, sponsored by Councilmember Farrah Lewis, would declare October as Reggaeton Heritage Month to honor the

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: legacy of reggaeton as a prominent expression of Afro-Caribbean and Latin American identity.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Introduction 927-A, sponsored by Councilmember Savina Brooks-Powers, would rename Shorefront Parkway between Beach

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: 32nd Street and Beach 56th Place to Edgemere Avenue and amend the official city map accordingly.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Introduction 786A, sponsored by also Councilmember Selena Brooks-Powers, would require the Commissioner of Correction to create procedures for curing ballots for voters in the custody of the Department of Correction.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers says Intro 786A will ensure voters in Rikers Island custody have their ballots counted. The bill requires DOC to check that envelopes are signed, dated, and contain the ballot before sending them to the Board of Elections, giving voters a chance to fix problems.
chapters.title: Selvena Brooks-Powers presents Intro 786A on ballot curing for voters in DOC custody

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And now I invite Councilmember Selena Brooks-Powers to the podium to discuss her legislation.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker Menon, and good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Today, the council will take a significant step to ensure that every vote in the city of New York matters.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: With the general election less than two weeks away, this is a reminder that every eligible New Yorker deserves a fair chance to make their vote count.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: My bill, Intro 786A, will ensure better accountability and give voters in custody at Rikers Island a fair chance to have their ballots counted.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Before the Department of Corrections sends a ballot to the Board of Elections, it will now have to check that the envelope is signed by the voter and anyone who helped the voter, dated, and contains the ballot.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: If a problem is found, the voter gets the chance and the means to fix it before the ballot goes out.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Most people held in our city's jails are awaiting trial and are presumed innocent, and they hold the same right to vote as any other eligible New Yorker.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Custody should never mean being denied the chance to have your voice heard.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Yet, for eligible New Yorkers in Department of Correction custody, voting by mail

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: is often the only option and for varying reasons participation has been extremely low.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Today the council will vote

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: on two bills to help close that gap.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you to my colleagues and the advocates for advancing this critical piece of legislation alongside another important bill that will be discussed being carried today by public advocate Jermani Williams and for your partnership in the work ahead.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We know that there is still much more work to do, including bringing a polling site to Rikers Island itself, but these two pieces of legislation are a major step in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Menin thanks Brooks-Powers and introduces Intro 905-A, sponsored by Councilmember Sandy Nurse. The bill gives not-for-profits a first opportunity to purchase certain residential properties, and Menin notes Nurse worked with stakeholders to address concerns and narrow the bill's scope.
chapters.title: Menin introduces Intro 905-A (COPA) and notes stakeholder revisions

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And then introduction 905-A, sponsored by Councilmember Sandy Nurse, would give certain not-for-profits or joint ventures between not-for-profits and other entities

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: a first opportunity to submit a statement of interest in purchasing and a first opportunity to purchase certain residential properties when offered for sale.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I want to mention that Councilmember Nurse has worked for many months to listen to stakeholder feedback.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The original bill, there were some council members who had concerns.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: There were some in industry who had concerns.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And she worked really collaboratively with council members and with industry to address those concerns and come up with a more targeted universe.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I appreciate the work that you did on this.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And now I invite Councilmember Nurse to the podium.

chapters.summary: Nurse says the Council is ending the six-year saga of the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act. She recalls COPA was first introduced in 2020 with a vision of keeping neighborhoods affordable when buildings are at risk.
chapters.title: Sandy Nurse announces end of six-year COPA saga

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Today we are going to end the six-year saga of the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act here in the Council, thanks to my colleagues, the relentless work of the New York City Community Land Initiative, and then, of course, to Speaker Menon.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: For those of you who don't know, COPA was first introduced in 2020 with a simple vision of neighborhoods that remained affordable because when buildings were at risk,

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: the people who live in them and the surrounding community would get a chance to fight for it.

chapters.summary: Nurse argues the housing crisis is not just about new construction, noting older affordable housing is being bought by private equity and house-flipping firms. She says 60% of New Yorkers cannot afford the basic cost of living and new construction cannot address displacement fast enough.
chapters.title: Nurse says private equity buying older affordable housing outpaces new construction

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And when we talk about the housing crisis, we often focus on new construction.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: But New York has quite a bit of older affordable.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: affordable housing that exists that is quickly being bought up by private equity and a lot of professional house flipping firms who then jack up the rent.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And 60% of New Yorkers cannot afford the basic cost of living here in this city.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: In fact, one in five people are reporting that they imagine themselves leaving here in the next five years because it just costs too much to stay.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: The fact is new construction can't answer that fast enough.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I just approved 1,000 units of 100% affordable housing in Broadway Junction last fall.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: That project's not coming online for at least a decade.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And working families just can't wait that long.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Buying and preserving some of the housing we already have is the most immediate way to stop displacement.

chapters.summary: Nurse says COPA lets trusted housing providers buy certain buildings, work with tenants, fix units, and keep tenants in place at permanently affordable rents. She says it gives landlords a pool of community-oriented buyers and brings buildings into public oversight.
chapters.title: Nurse explains how COPA lets community providers preserve affordable housing

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And that's what COPA does.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It lets trusted housing providers buy certain buildings, work with those tenants, fix the units up, and put those tenants back in those same units and keep them there at permanently affordable rents.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It gives eligible landlords a pool of community-oriented buyers who know this work.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And it brings those buildings into a form of public oversight.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: In the hottest real estate market in the country where transactions happen very quickly and often with cash, we are going to offer some New Yorkers an opportunity to stay.

chapters.summary: Nurse says COPA has been through three mayors, introduced four times, heard three times, passed, vetoed, and faced intense real estate lobbying. She says when she inherited the bill 13 months ago it was stuck, and the version being voted on is the strongest and most operationally sound yet.
chapters.title: Nurse recounts COPA's history through three mayors, veto, and lobbying

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: The bill has been through the fire.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It has been through three mayors.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It's been introduced four times.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It's been heard three times.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It got passed.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It got passed.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: vetoed.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It has sustained a really intense lobbying effort by the real estate lobby to stop the bill.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And when I inherited the bill about 13 months ago, it was truly stuck in gridlock, the original bill.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And we had to really start over again and negotiate a bill and a program that is workable.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And I say all that to say that I believe the version that we are voting on today is the strongest, most strategic, and most operationally sound version of COPA yet.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And I am just extremely proud to head into the chambers to vote for this today.

chapters.summary: Nurse thanks her chief Ryan, the Progressive Caucus, and Speaker Menin for trusting her to renegotiate COPA. She says she is proud to vote for it today.
chapters.title: Nurse thanks team and Progressive Caucus for COPA passage

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: There's a lot of people I want to thank.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: We had a brilliant bill drafting team.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: My chief, Ryan, who's here, who spent hours of his life on this.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: The Progressive Caucus that championed this for five years in the council.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And of course, to Speaker Menon, thank you for trusting me to renegotiate this and work with my colleagues to earn their trust.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And I'm proud to be voting on this today.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Menin thanks Nurse and introduces Intro 797A, sponsored by Public Advocate Jumaane Williams. The bill would require the Department of Correction to annually report on voter registration and voting activities in city jails.
chapters.title: Menin introduces Intro 797A on DOC voter registration reporting

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Introduction 797A, sponsored by Public Advocate Jumaane Williams, would require DOC to annually report on the number of voter registration and voting activities in city jails.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I now invite Public Advocate Williams to the podium to discuss his legislation.

chapters.summary: Williams greets the room and notes press interest in voting on Rikers Island. He says early voting is two days away and election day is less than two weeks away, making protection of voting rights essential.
chapters.title: Jumaane Williams opens on voting rights and press interest in Rikers

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Peace and blessings.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Love and light.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm a speaker.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm excited to see how many press are interested in voting in Rikers Island.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: They're out here today.

chapters.summary: Williams says some politicians benefit when people cannot vote and points to disenfranchisement of Black and brown voters. He says thousands of eligible voters on Rikers Island lack equitable ballot access, and this goes largely unchallenged.
chapters.title: Williams says Rikers voters face systemic disenfranchisement

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: With early voting two days away and election day in less than two weeks, we know that protecting the rights and ability of people to vote is essential.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Some politicians seem to believe that when you don't think you can earn someone's vote, it's easy if they can't vote at all.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And we, of course, are seeing black and brown voters disenfranchised across the South.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We often say you don't have to look that far.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: You can just look into the East River.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thousands of eligible voters on Rikers Island are not given equitable access to the ballot.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We would not accept the systemic disenfranchising of eligible voters anywhere else in the city, yet it goes largely unseen and unchallenged in our jails.

chapters.summary: Williams says Rikers Island reflects failures of government leadership and that nearly 7,000 detained people, most pre-trial or serving misdemeanor time, are eligible to vote. He says only a fraction successfully cast ballots because there are no polling sites and absentee voting is unreliable.
chapters.title: Williams details low ballot access for nearly 7,000 detained on Rikers

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In many ways, Wackett Island is evidence of failures of government leadership.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Yet so many of the people detained there have no voice in changing that government or holding it accountable.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: There are close to 7,000 people detained on Rikers Island, most of whom are being detained pre-trial or serving time for Mr.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Veeners and therefore

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: are eligible to vote.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Despite this, only a fraction of the incarcerated population in the jail successfully cast a ballot.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: As there are no polling sites at Rikers, detained voters must rely on the absentee ballot process, which is the responsibility of the Board of Elections and Department of Corrections.

chapters.summary: Williams says Intro 797A would require DOC to report on voter registration forms, absentee ballots distributed, voting events, and demographic information. He says the next step is a polling site on Rikers and asks the Council to vote aye.
chapters.title: Williams presents Intro 797A reporting requirements and calls for Rikers polling site

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So today I'm proud to have the council voting on my bill, Intro 797A, alongside Intro 786A, sponsored by Councilmember Sabina Brooks-Powers, which you heard

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: previously, to understand the voting landscape in Rikers, hold our city accountable for gaps in voter outreach, and ensure every ballot is counted.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: My bill will require DOC to report on the number of voter registration and voting activities, including the numbers of completed voter registration forms, absentee ballots distributed to incarcerated individuals, and events held to promote voting

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: in city jails, as well as on demographic information of people returning voter registration forms to the department.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Expanding ballot access would not only strengthen voting rights for incarcerated New Yorkers, but also support public safety efforts to address mass incarceration of these communities, as voting has been related to reducing recidivism.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I believe the next step is a polling site on Rikers, but to get there we need this information, and we ask the council to stand up for democracy every way and vote aye.

chapters.summary: Williams says over 80% of people on Rikers are awaiting trial and most will return to the community. He argues keeping them civically engaged reduces recidivism and thanks Speaker Menin and Councilmember Brooks-Powers.
chapters.title: Williams argues civic engagement reduces recidivism and thanks colleagues

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Always want to remind folks that over 80% of the folks who are there are simply waiting for trial.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: A vast majority of them will return to the community having never served time of state.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: These folks will return to the community the more that we can keep them civically engaged.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And connected to the community is the better.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So this should be a thing that all New Yorkers support.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We want to make sure that people come back home better than when they were there.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And right now, that's not what's happening.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I just want to thank Speaker Menon for her leadership.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank Councilmember Brooks-Powers for her leadership.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And thank you for the council hopefully be passing this in a few hours.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Menin thanks Williams and introduces Intro 853A, sponsored by Councilmember Susan Zhuang. The bill would require the Department of Education to supplement special education reporting with analysis of factors affecting access and recommendations to address barriers.
chapters.title: Menin introduces Intro 853A on special education reporting

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Introduction 853A, sponsored by Councilmember Susan Zhuang, would require the Department of Education to supplement existing special education reporting

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: with analysis on how certain factors affect students'access to special education programs and services and to report recommendations on how to address any identified barriers to that access.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So now invite Councilmember Zhuang to talk about her bill.

chapters.summary: Zhuang thanks colleagues for passing her first bill, Intro 684, on gifted and talented access. She says Intro 853A is a sister bill to ensure every child can access the special education program they need.
chapters.title: Susan Zhuang presents Intro 853A as sister bill to gifted and talented access

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I also want to thank my colleagues to passing my first bill, Intro 684, in my Access for All package, which is two weeks ago, and expanding

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: equitable access to gifted and talented programs.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Today we are going to vote my, it's a sister bill, Intro 8.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: 853 to help ensure every child access the special education program they need.

chapters.summary: Zhuang recalls a December 2025 incident where a school bus with six nonverbal special education students went missing for over four hours. She says too many children travel long bus rides, and language barriers and family income make navigating the system harder.
chapters.title: Zhuang cites missing school bus and barriers for special education students

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: On December 16, 2025, we all see on the news a school bus carrying six nonverbal special ed students aged from

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: six to eight when missing for more than four hours.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: As a mother, I cannot imagine the fear those families suffered.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Too many children in outborough have to travel long buses, long bus ride to reach the service they need.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Meanwhile, language barriers and the family income can make it even harder

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: for parents to navigate the system.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We cannot wait to address this inequities.

chapters.summary: Zhuang says Intro 853A requires the city to annually study how geography, income, and language access affect special education access. She says the data will identify gaps and ensure no child is left behind because of zip code, income, or home language.
chapters.title: Zhuang says Intro 853A will study geographic, income, and language barriers

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: In intro 853, requires the city to study annually how geographic income and language access affect access to special education programs and services.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We need this data to identify the gaps and find solutions.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: No child should be left behind because their zip code or their family income or the language they speak at home.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Every child deserves access to education they need to succeed, no matter their special needs or super talented.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Menin introduces Intro 296A, sponsored by Councilmember Farah Louis, requiring a report on gender-based violence data collection. She also introduces Intro 978B, also by Louis, raising the SCRIE and DRIE income limit to $75,000 beginning July 1, 2026.
chapters.title: Menin introduces Intro 296A and 978B on gender-based violence data and SCRIE/DRIE

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Introduction 296A, sponsored by Councilmember Farrah Lewis, would require the Mayor's Office to end gender-based violence in consultation with the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: to develop a report with recommendations for agencies to improve the collection and integration of data on gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Introduction 978B, also sponsored by Councilmember Farrah Lewis, would increase the maximum income level for eligibility for the Senior Citizen Rent Increase Exemption Program

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: and the Disability Rent Increase Exemption Program to $75,000 beginning July 1, 2026.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I now invite Councilmember Lewis to the podium to discuss her bills.

chapters.summary: Louis says New Yorkers face life-changing challenges and government must protect the vulnerable. She cites Nathalie Ramirez, who reportedly was pushed from a balcony while holding her baby, and says Intro 296 will help identify patterns of abuse and coordinate responses.
chapters.title: Farah Louis links gender-based violence data bill to Nathalie Ramirez tragedy

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you so much, Speaker Menon, for your leadership and for advancing these important bills.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Everyday New Yorkers face challenges that can change their lives in an instant.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Our responsibility is to ensure that when they are most vulnerable, our systems are prepared to protect them.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: On October 6, Nathalie Ramirez reportedly lost her life after being pushed from her 15th floor balcony while holding her baby.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Her child survived.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Reports of her former partner's history of domestic violence would make this tragedy even more heartbreaking.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Nathalie's story reminds us that leaving an abusive relationship does not always mean the danger is over.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: We must do more to recognize patterns of abuse, coordinate our responses, and intervene before another family experiences this kind of loss.

chapters.summary: Louis says Intro 296 brings together gender-based violence data to strengthen prevention and direct resources. She says Intro 976 raises the SCRIE and DRIE income eligibility limit from $50,000 to $75,000, helping older adults and people with disabilities stay in their homes.
chapters.title: Louis explains Intro 296 data integration and Intro 976 rent exemption increase

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Intro 296 helps us to take this step by bringing together data on gender-based violence so we can better identify gaps, strengthen prevention, and direct resources where they are needed most.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: By protecting New Yorkers also means protecting their ability to remain in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Imagine spending decades building a life here in New York City only to find yourself struggling to afford an apartment you call home.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: For many older adults and people with disabilities,

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Disabilities, rising rents, health care costs, and everyday expenses makes that fear a reality.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Intro 976 raises the income eligibility limit for scree and dree from $50,000 to $75,000,

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: allowing more eligible New Yorkers access to rent protections and remain in their homes with greater security.

chapters.summary: Louis says the bills address different challenges but share the principle that no New Yorker should be left vulnerable because systems fail to recognize their needs. She says policies must protect survivors of violence, older adults, and people with disabilities with dignity.
chapters.title: Louis says policies must protect vulnerable New Yorkers with dignity

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: These bills address different challenges, but the principle is all the same.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: No New Yorker should be left vulnerable because our systems fail to recognize their needs.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Whether we are protecting survivors of violence or helping older adults or folks with disabilities with dignity, our policies must reflect the lives here of the city and to protect those in need.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Menin thanks Louis and introduces Intro 943A, sponsored by Councilmember Christopher Marte. The bill would prohibit issuance of licenses for carriage horses, horse-drawn cabs, and horse-drawn cab drivers on or after June 1, 2028.
chapters.title: Menin introduces Intro 943A to wind down horse carriage industry

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And then, finally, Introduction 943A, sponsored by Councilmember Christopher Marte, would wind down the horse carriage industry by prohibiting the issuance of licenses for carriage horses,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: horse-drawn cabs, and horse-drawn cab drivers on or after June 1, 2028.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Now I invite Councilmember Marte to the podium to discuss his legislation.

chapters.summary: Marte thanks colleagues and notes the ASPCA was formed 160 years ago to care for horses. He says after over two centuries of advocacy, the Council is finally voting to end horse carriages in Central Park.
chapters.title: Christopher Marte opens on ASPCA history and ending horse carriages

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker, and thank you to all my colleagues who have been supportive of this.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: 160 years ago, ASPCA was formed here in New York City to do one thing, to take care of horses.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And they advocated and organized for over two centuries through a number of names, whether it's Nye Class or PETA, to end horse carriages in Central Park.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And today, we're finally taking a vote to make that happen.

chapters.summary: Marte says Intro 943A will transition horses to sanctuaries, prevent sales to slaughterhouses or other carriage industries, and protect workers. The bill requires agencies to create transition packages with training, employment referrals to TLC and MTA, career counseling, and job training.
chapters.title: Marte details horse sanctuary, slaughter ban, and worker transition in Intro 943A

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Bill, intro 943A, would do a...

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: few things.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: It will make sure that the horses can transition to sanctuaries by not allowing them to be sold to other slaughterhouses or other industries that have horse carriages related to it.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: It will also protect the worker, which makes this a win-win, not just for animal welfare, but for workers'rights.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: The bill will propose agencies to, or demand agencies to create a package of potential transition, which will take into consideration training and employment referrals to similar industries like the TLC and the MTA.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And most recently, we just heard from the head of the MTA, who is open to help these workers find new jobs within that agency.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: But it will also create career counseling and job training programs for the drivers and workers.

chapters.summary: Marte says the union in the horse carriage industry only represents owners, while many drivers and stable workers are independent contractors. He says the bill will work with the administration on a holistic approach for everyone in the industry.
chapters.title: Marte notes union represents owners while drivers are independent contractors

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And I think there's something important that has to be mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: The union in this industry only represents the owners.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Many of the drivers, many of the people that work in the stables are independent contractors.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And so what we will do in this bill is make sure that we work with the administration to find a holistic approach for everyone who works in this industry.

chapters.summary: Marte thanks everyone who worked over 30 years on the issue. He notes the bill was first introduced by former Councilmember Tony Avella, then taken over by former Councilmember Bob Holden, and he took it over earlier this year to create a win-win solution for horses and workers.
chapters.title: Marte thanks supporters and recounts bill's history

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: I want to thank everyone who's worked over 30 years on this.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: The bill, as the Speaker mentioned, was first introduced close to two decades ago by former Councilmember Tony Aviles.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: It was taken over by former Councilmember Bob Holden.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And when I took over this bill earlier this year, I spoke to the Speaker's team, and we really wanted to make this a win-win solution, one that...

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Text the animals, the horses who have given so much to our city, but also to make sure that the workers have a just transition to new careers.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker, and thank you to the council.

chapters.summary: Menin thanks Councilmember Marte and announces that concludes the stated agenda.
chapters.title: Menin thanks Marte and concludes stated agenda

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember March.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Hey, so that concludes our stated agenda.

chapters.summary: Asked about claims the horse carriage bill is unconstitutional at the state and federal level, Menin says she is confident in the legislation. She says the Council worked over the summer, strengthened worker protections, and will vigorously defend the law.
chapters.title: Menin defends horse carriage bill against constitutional concerns

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Is this something that you're concerned about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They've talked about the bill being unconstitutional at the state and federal level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, just one more question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We're very confident in the legislation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That's why we took the time to work over the summer on the legislation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We made changes to the legislation to beef up the worker protection.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We are very confident in defending this law and will vigorously defend it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I've already talked to Steve Banks about it and our team, and we will vigorously defend this law.

chapters.summary: Asked why the Adams veto on COPA was allowed to stand, Menin cites a law department memo raising concerns. She says the property universe was narrowed to about 2,100 buildings from 10,000, making the bill more targeted. Nurse adds the December version was legally sound, and changes were mainly to help HPD operationalize the program.
chapters.title: Menin and Nurse explain COPA changes after law department concerns

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, I just wanted to ask about COPA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: One of your first moves as speaker was to allow the Eric Adams veto on the past iteration to stand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You mentioned that things have changed, state of the response, all of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Is there anything that you can speak to that specifically changed?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So first of all, when I became speaker, we received a memo from the law department that had raised concerns about COPA.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That memo hit my desk right after I became speaker.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We raised those legal concerns, and I really think that we've now thoughtfully taken the time working with the bill sponsor, working with the industry, working with council members and other stakeholders.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The universe of properties was narrowed to about 2,100 buildings from the original approximately 10,000.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So it has been narrowed and it's a more targeted approach.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And that is why a lot of different...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Whether it be industry or council members who initially had opposed it, are now more comfortable with this new version, and we were able to address some of the legal issues that the law department had raised, and we made a more targeted bill.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Yeah, and just to have an accurate picture, you know, the version we passed in December, the law department said was legally sound.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It was more that there was a number of different points that could be sued over.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So it wasn't that there was anything unconstitutional in it.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It's just they wanted an opportunity to restrengthen now that they've had a third review of it.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: The changes that were made were largely on behalf of the city agency and their ability to operationalize this program rather than the private sector.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: This was about working with HPD and making sure that what we created is a precise universe so we can have very accurate communications with COPA-eligible landlords.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So I feel good about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Asked why the horse carriage bill only considers creating a compensation program for medallion owners, Menin says it is up to the administration. She says the language was agreed to with the administration, worker protections were strengthened, and the administration will develop the plan.
chapters.title: Menin explains why horse carriage worker compensation is 'consider' not guaranteed

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Speaker, I was wondering why the bill to ban horse carriages is only, it only has language about considering creating a program to compensate the workers for their medallions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Why only consider it instead of guaranteeing it?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Well, yeah, thanks, Chris, for the question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, that is going to be up to the administration.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We basically, from the time we had the hearing to the time of the vote, our legislative team was in discussion with the legislative team of the administration to come up with language.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We were very clear we wanted to strengthen the worker protection language, which was strengthened from the original bill.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And then it is now up to the administration to work on that plan, a plan that basically compensates the medallion owners, a plan that ensures that these workers have jobs.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So that we're going to work very closely with the administration on it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But to be clear, that was language that, you know, was worked out with the administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So they want the door to be had less considered as opposed to guaranteed?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, this was language that was agreed to with their team.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Because, again, it's going to be the administration that has to implement it, so they need to be comfortable with that language.

chapters.summary: Asked whether Ramach Mahajan's death is the critical factor and why not act immediately on e-bikes, Menin says the Council is taking immediate action. She says it heard 23 e-bike bills over the summer, will ban Class 3 e-bikes, and is working on licensing, insurance, and age verification.
chapters.title: Menin defends urgency of horse carriage ban amid e-bike fatality questions

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You said, I believe, in your remarks about the horse carriage bill, that the death of Ramachan was one death too many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I know some of the critics of this bill, including the carriage drivers, have pointed out that there have been a few fatal incidents involving e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Is there, is it the death of Ramach Mahajan that is like the critical factor making it urgent to pass this legislation now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Or is it more in your mind about the welfare of the horses and if one death too many in the carriage industry is enough to ban it, why not take immediate action related to the e-bike?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Well, we are taking immediate action on the e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That's why over the summer we heard 23 bills, which I think is the most the council has ever heard on any topic, on e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And to be clear, we will ban those Class 3 e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That is something that those e-bikes are illegally going up to 25 miles an hour.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: They're causing a lot of the injuries and deaths that we're seeing, and we will ban them.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We also have other bills that require licensing from third-party apps to bring, whether it's Uber Eats or DoorDash, but the third-party apps under regulatory purview.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We have another bill on insurance.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We have a bill that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's in drafting right now, and it will be shortly introduced on age verification for city people.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: because I think it's unacceptable that teenagers are riding city bike, and it's really a safety concern for them.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So soup to nuts.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We have, I'm not going to mention all 23 bills.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We have a lot of bills.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So we are going to pass the e-bike package immediately.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We've been working on taking the changes from the hearing, adding them to the bills, and those bills are going to move forward very, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And then, yeah.

chapters.summary: Menin reviews past attempts to regulate horse carriages and says the Central Park Conservancy's opposition was significant. She cites spooked horses, 42 million annual visitors, and Ramaj Mahajan's death as factors creating a tipping point, and says the Council is taking a comprehensive public safety approach to e-bikes, pedicabs, and horse carriages.
chapters.title: Menin cites Central Park Conservancy and spooked horses as factors for carriage ban

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Well, I think if you go back and look at the original council legislation on the horse carriage industry, there has been a multitude of different bills every few years to regulate this industry

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: around working in high temperatures, around having a mandated veterinary appointment.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So over the years, there have been attempts by the council to try to regulate it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But now when the Central Park Conservancy last year came out against this, that to me was a significant factor.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: When this year alone, you had numerous instances of the horses being spooked and breaking free and causing not only a danger to themselves, but to the pedestrians that are in the park.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: When 42 million people come to Central Park each and every year, and the horses are operating in a very small area.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And then sadly, in June, when Ramaj Mahajan lost his life thrown from a horse, I think it's a multitude of factors that required a tipping point.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And to be clear, from a public safety standpoint, we are going to crack down on the illegal use of the dangerous high-speed e-bikes that are going 25 miles an hour, or 20 miles an hour, that are totally unacceptable and shouldn't be sold.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We're going to work on the insurance.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We're working on the third-party licensing.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We're working on age verification for young riders of city bike.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we're also working on pedicabs.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So we are soup to nuts, taking a comprehensive public safety approach.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Of dealing with the pedicab issue, the e-bike issue, and the horse carriage issue.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We are doing all three.

chapters.summary: Menin explains that horse owners must certify to the Department of Health what will happen to their horses, and they can keep them but cannot use them for carriage or send them to slaughter. Marte adds owners must give 10-day notice before a sale and cannot sell to slaughterhouses, other carriage industries, or resellers.
chapters.title: Menin and Marte detail horse sale certification and slaughter ban

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Oh, sure.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So basically, under the bill, and I'll also turn to Councilmember Marte after I speak to add some additional context for this, but it requires that the owners of a horse have to provide a certification to the Department of Health about

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: what will happen with the horse.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: To be clear, if the owner wants to keep the horse, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We in no way want to separate owners from their horses.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It just cannot be used for a horse-drawn carriage, and it cannot be sent to slaughter.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So they have to provide that certification.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And so let me turn it over to Councilor Marches.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Is there something you want to add on that?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Yeah, I think the speaker covered most of it.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: So in the bill, the owner of the horses have to give a 10-day heads up before they actually conduct a sale to the administration.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And as the speaker said, they can't be sold to a slaughterhouse, they can't be sold to another horse carriage industry, or they can't be sold to someone who's going to resell it to a slaughterhouse, making sure that we can protect the horses as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Hi, Sally.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, I will answer that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I guess we'll go to the on topic and then I'll answer because I absolutely have an answer on that.

chapters.summary: Asked what is uniquely cruel about horse carriages compared to other animal industries, Menin says horses pull up to 1,000 pounds in hot, crowded Central Park. She notes the Council has acted on puppy mills and created an animal welfare caucus chaired by Councilmember Epstein.
chapters.title: Menin defends horse carriage ban against comparison to slaughterhouses and kill shelters

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So if, you know, Laura kind of asked my first question, but my second one is...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, there are many industries in New York City that animal welfare advocates take issue with, including kill shelters, which are run by the city, including slaughterhouses, which are regulated by the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: What is so uniquely cruel about the horse carriages that demands the elimination of the industry?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the horses are pulling sometimes up to 1,000 pounds, which comprises the carriages and people in it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Oftentimes in hot summer months, we are seeing that in an area that has 42 million visitors a year, they're operating in a very crowded area, which is one of the reasons the Central Park Conservancy came out

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: well over a year ago to say they did not think that they could continue to operate in the park.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And so I think there are real issues around that, and that is one of the motivating factors behind the bill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But how is pulling a thousand pound carriage worse than being slaughtered?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the council acted on other animal welfare issues, puppy mills, things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So it's not as if the council has not done that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I think we now have an animal welfare caucus for the first time, which I appointed and Councilmember Epstein is the chair of it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I'm sure they are going to be engaging in additional efforts on other issues.

chapters.summary: Asked about the driver's union claim that there are no economic impact details, Menin says the Council met repeatedly with TWU, workers, and medallion owners. She says the administration will be responsible for ensuring workers get jobs and protecting medallion owners' rights. Marte notes past administrations have offered transition packages.
chapters.title: Menin and Marte address economic impact and worker transition for carriage industry

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Hi, the driver's union said that there was no details about the economic impact of the horse carriage business.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Can you explain what it is?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Sure, sure.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Well, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So there are details in the sense that we have repeatedly met with TWU.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We have met with workers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We have met with medallion owners.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: For months, we've had meetings with them.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And with the administration, now that they are the ones that are going to be responsible for this plan, and so that language was agreed to with the administration in terms of the administration will take the responsibility

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: on.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Ensuring that all of the workers get jobs because that has to happen.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That is mission critical.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: These workers deserve to have their job protected.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It absolutely has to happen.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And then also the rights of the medallion owners as well.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Did you want to say something else?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I think you want to add something.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Just the final thing is, like, historically, administrations have been the one to offer a package to this industry.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: We saw it at the end of the Adams administration, but we also saw it previous to that in the de Blasio administration, where they took the onus to offer something to the industry.

chapters.summary: Menin says a pending bill is important and worker protections are at stake. She says the law department sent additional red lines, the Council will meet with the Urban League, and it is concerned about rising consumer costs, including Amazon Pharmacy prices, and small businesses losing business.
chapters.title: Menin discusses law department red lines and consumer cost concerns on pending bill

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, Sally.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I think that this is a very important bill.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Obviously, we need to protect these workers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: There are enormous worker protection issues at stake.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: What we're doing now is we're in conversation with the law department.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The law department sent over some additional red lines.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This morning, I believe, or late last night.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: One of the things that I'm interested in focusing on is having conversations to address some of the concerns about the bill.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The Urban League had indicated some concerns they have, so we will meet with them to hear them out.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We also are focused on rising consumer costs, so we want to see if there's a way to somehow address that as well.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Because, for example, numerous city workers and New Yorkers use Amazon Pharmacy to get their pharmaceuticals.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So we don't want a situation where suddenly then Amazon tries to jack up those costs.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So those are issues that we're working through.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we're continuing to have those conversations.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yeah, we have to.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And they're also, we're working with the law department to resolve some of the legal issues around the bill.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So there's more to come on that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's a process.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And so we're working through.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's not that the law department, I don't want to say something that's not.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We, for any bill, and we did this, for example, around other bills that we work with the law department, we want to make sure that the language works.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And right now, that's a process that we're undergoing with them right now.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So we're in conversations with the law department on that bill.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: At the same time, we also want to make sure that consumer prices are not going to rise because that's very, very important.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And so we want to be able to address that concern.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We also want to address a concern about these small businesses to make sure that they're not losing their business.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So all of these different factors, we're taking that in, and we will be working on this.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I'm committed to working on it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We want to address the consumer price issue.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We want to address the small business issue to make sure that these businesses are not losing those businesses and that people are not losing their jobs and that Amazon then does not try to jack up people's pharmaceutical prices and other consumer goods.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I believe we can address those issues.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm confident that we can address.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: There are myriad issues.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm confident we can address them.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And once we've addressed them, then we'll address it at that point.

chapters.summary: Asked about Mayor Zoram Moudani signing only one bill and leaving over 100 on his desk, Menin says it is up to the mayor whether to hold bill signings. She says bill signings are great opportunities to amplify issues and hear from the public, hopes he does more, and has not talked to him about it.
chapters.title: Menin responds to mayor's low bill-signing record

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm just wondering, yesterday it was reported that the mayor, Zoram Moudani, has only signed one bill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: He's left over 100 questions on his desk over the 10 months of his term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: As the leader of this body, can you just tell me your opinion on that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Do you find it offensive, given all the work that the council has done to pass these bills?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Look, it's up to the mayor if he wants to do a bill signing or not.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, I've served as commissioner of several agencies over the years.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I've gone to a lot of bill signings, not only as a council member, but as a commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I think bill signings are great because I think it's an important opportunity to amplify the issue and also hear from the public in that public hearing that happens before the bill signing.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I think bill signings are great.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I hope he does more moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I haven't.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: No, I have not talked to him about that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And that's up to him if he wants to do a bill signing or not.

chapters.summary: Asked about vandalism at a Capitol One Bank and a weapons manufacturer, Menin says it is up to the NYPD to investigate. She says the 19th Precinct indicated it was investigating as a hate crime and sending it to the hate crime division, and the Council is not privy to all facts.
chapters.title: Menin comments on vandalism investigation as possible anti-Semitic hate crime

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Hi, hi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So this vandalism of the Capitol One Bank, the L.D., weapons manufacturer, and how actually culture is investigated as an anti-Semitic hate crime, do you think that's an anti-Semitic message?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Oh, no, I don't think it's, I think basically that's up to the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The NYPD needs to investigate it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: When we talked to the 19th Precinct, they indicated that they were investigating it as a hate crime, and it was being sent to the hate crime division.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But that's up to them to determine.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We don't know all the facts behind other things are happening.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's vandalism.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That's what it is.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And so it needs to, and so they're investigating it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And so we'll learn more once they have an announcement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But you called for it to be investigated as an anti-Semitic case.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Well, that's after conversation with the 19th Precinct where they said that that was what they were doing for investigation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We are not privy to all the facts around the case.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So we were amplifying what we were told by the 19th Precinct.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

summary: Speaker Julie Menin opens with policy announcements on homeowner stabilization, free 2K expansion, EMS response times, SCRIE/DRIE increases, and the horse carriage phase-out bill.
Council members present legislation on COPA, voting access for people in DOC custody, special education reporting, gender-based violence data, rent exemptions, and ending horse carriages.
A press Q&A follows, covering the horse carriage bill's constitutionality and worker compensation, COPA changes, e-bike safety, the mayor's bill-signing record, and a vandalism investigation.
